To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(a) there is no significant correlation between the number of choline acetyltransferase‐positive neurons in the MS/vDB and the density of choline acetyltansferase‐positive fibers in the hippocampus, and (b) the number of parvalbumin immunopositive neurons in the MS/DB is significantly correlated with the density of cholecytolinergic fibers in CA1.

the extent of the intra‐ and infrapiramidal mossy fiber projections in different mouse strains is correlated with the extent of septal cholinergic innervation and with the extent of GABAergic innervation of the hippocampus.
the extent of the septal‐hippocampus projections and the number of parvalbumin containing neurons in the MS/vDB were correlated with the spatial and activity‐dependent learning and memory variables.
In summary, our research is concerned with

the question of the extent to which genetic variation in the morphology and functioning of the septohippocampic cholinergic and γ‐aminobutyric acidergic (GABAergic) system is related to spatial learning and memory in mice.

the genetic and environmental factors that contribute to the morphological variation of the septo-hippocampo-prefrontal cholinergic projection system and the hippocampal GABAergic system and with the behavioral consequences of this variation.
the genetic variation of the morphology of the central cholinergic and gamma-aminobutyric acid (GABA) systems and the correlation between these variations and behavior.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the septo‐hpcampal GABAergic and cholinergic systems are not involved in the regulation of spatial and nonspacial memory and learning in mice.

the extent of the intra‐ and infrapirymidal mossy fiber projections in the hippocampus is not the sole determinant of spatial and nonsppatial aspects of learning and/or memory, and that the septo‐hypocampal cholineergic and GABAergetic system is not the only system involved in the regulation of spatial and non‐spatial aspects of memory and learning.

, although there are significant correlations of some of the morphometric parameters with the behavioral variables, the contribution of the investigated cholinergic and/or GABAergic markers to the behavioral performance is rather modest.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

the cholinergic septo‐hippoampal system is not involved in learning and memory processes in mice, whereas the GABAergic septo‐ hippocampal system seems to be involved in the acquisition of spatial working memory.

the extent of the intra‐ and infrapiramidal mossy fiber projections in the hippocampus of different inbred mouse lines was found to correlate positively with the number of septal cholinergic neurons and with the extent of cholinergic innervation in the CA1 and CA3 subfield of the hippocampus.

the septo‐hypocampal cholineergic and GABAeric systems are important determinants of spatial and nonspacial learning and memory, but the contribution of the two systems to these functions is different.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the extent of the cholinergic innervation of the hippocampus and of the parvalbumin expression in the MS/vDB are the main determinants of spatial memory in mice.
the extent of the septohippocampalmossy fiber projection is not the only morphological variable that correlates with behavioral performance.
the septo‐hypocampal cholineergic system plays a more important role in spatial than in nonspatial memory, whereas the septo‐pyramidal GABAergic system seems to be involved in both.
